newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Bolivia leader wins poll making promises to poor.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia leader wins poll making promises to poor.

text.p: Ex-dictator Hugo Banzer clinched a first round of voting and looked set to become Bolivia's next president by tapping discontent with economic policies that hit the poor too hard, analysts said on Monday.

Bankers and human rights activists agreed Banzer won the Sunday vote by concentrating his political firepower on the negative effects of President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada's free-market and privatisation drive.
"Riches have concentrated on the top of the social pyramid," the 71-year-old right-wing general told Reuters in an interview hours before the vote.

An unofficial but complete count of Sunday's election showed Banzer of the Nationalist Democratic Action (ADN) in first place and Juan Carlos Duran of the ruling, centrist Nationalist Revolutionary Movement (MNR) second.

Congress selects the winner in early August and will be theoretically free to pick any of the top two candidates. But Banzer's party did much better in legislative elections, virtually guaranteeing him a victory.

Analysts say the reason he did so well despite his human rights record -- he led a military regime for seven years after seizing power in a coup in 1971-- was his stance on economic issues. He has endorsed the 12-year-old free-market and privatisation drive that is highly praised by the international financial community but appears to be testing the limits of Bolivians' patience.

Sensing the discontent with railways, telephones and services whose post-privatisation rates have shot up beyond the reach of many Bolivians, 70 percent of whom live under the poverty line, Banzer promised to try to put an end to private firm monopolies and "humanize" the economy.
"People feel that, because of the monopolies, (privatization) has hurt rather than benefitted them," said Chamber of Industries General Manager Carlos Alberto Lopez.

Former Central Bank President Armando Mendez said both people in the street and the business community endorsed Banzer's plans to review the privatisation contracts. He has also promised better access to education, credit and jobs for Bolivians, half of whom are pure-blooded Aymara and Quechua Indians who still speak the tongue of their ancestors. Nearly 40 percent of the population is illiterate.

Banzer says soft credit and training should help improve the lot of 1.9 million people who lack a steady job. Many of them are native Bolivians who left their homelands for the cities where they offer goods for sale on the streets.

But human rights advocates lament that what they see as a legitimate demand for a change of economic tack would result in the election of the general. "He represents a 7-year de facto regime marked by ... torture, exile, disappearances and state-terrorism," said Waldo Albarracin, president of the Permanent Human Rights Assembly.

After winning the vote Sunday, Banzer admitted he had acted in an authoritarian way and promised that as president he would respect the constitution and serve the Bolivian people, especially the poor.
Albarracin also said he found no real cures to the plight of the poor in Banzer's proposals, just cosmetic changes. "It's the same Indian with a different poncho," he said.
